request.prompt: Which humanoid robots have SDK access?

result.text:
A growing number of humanoid and bipedal robotic platforms offer software development kits (SDKs), ranging from open-source research platforms to enterprise-restricted industrial units.

1. Open-Source & Research-Focused Humanoid SDKs

Unitree G1 (EDU / Standard Series)

SDK / API: Uses unitree_sdk2 (C++ & Python) supporting secondary development on its dedicated computing unit, alongside ROS 2 and Cyclone DDS integration.
Ecosystem: Well-supported in simulation environments like MuJoCo and NVIDIA Isaac Lab.
Source Info: Detailed via the Unitree G1 Developer Guide.

Pollen Robotics Reachy 2

SDK / API: Built with a native ROS 2 stack and an Apache 2.0 open-source software license. Features a VR-based teleoperation SDK for bimanual manipulation research.
Ecosystem: Tailored for academic and laboratory research published in robotics venues.
Source Info: Outlined in the Robotics Center Open-Source Humanoid Guide.

Booster Robotics K1 (Geek Edition)

SDK / API: Offers secondary development access and motion control interfaces, sometimes bundled with integrated LLM development hooks.
Source Info: Referenced via marketplace and technical roundups like Joybuy Developer Insights.

2. Commercial / Industrial Humanoid Platforms (Restricted or Partner-Only SDKs)

Agility Robotics (Digit)

SDK / API: Historically restricted to commercial pilot partners, research institutions under specific agreements, or Agility's cloud/API automation layer (Digit Arc) rather than a public, open download.

Figure AI (Figure 01 / Figure 02)

SDK / API: Uses a proprietary, closed-source motion and vision-language model (VLM) stack. Public SDK access is generally unavailable, limited instead to strategic commercial deployments (e.g., automotive manufacturing partners).

Tesla (Optimus)

SDK / API: Closed ecosystem tightly integrated into Tesla’s internal software stack; no public or third-party developer SDK has been released.

Boston Dynamics (Atlas — Electric/Commercial transition)

SDK / API: Historically managed via exclusive academic research programs (like the old Boston Dynamics API or ROS wrappers for older Spot/Atlas generations), with modern commercial humanoid iterations strictly controlled via enterprise partnerships.

If you are looking to build for a specific use case—such as academic research, industrial automation, or simulation-first prototyping—let me know your budget or technical requirements and I can point you toward the best-fit platform.
